title: Four verdicts about the same subject (worked out on cardboard)
note: The authored thinking for one hall, in the first person, by the pass (Claude), for Palle's request of 2026-11-14 (see Russell_Paradox.json). 'at' is the floor's own frame in metres (x east, z south), 'yaw' in degrees. A sticker of kind 'quote' stands word for word in the hall text; every other kind is mine and may be wrong - the plates say where I am unsure.

hero.why: The four inward-facing panels are the hall's whole text: one subject, four authored verdicts with supplied confidences and an address, and controls that hide or dress the address. The panel that says DANGEROUS is the one the text stays with.
hero.staging: The four panels already stood round the arrival inside the installed camera bay, and the pass moved none of them (f7c2435ba moved only the creature's starting place). The plates stand outside the bay: two at the south corners, three along the south band to the east wing, four round the stations.

plates.title: 1  THE SUBJECT STAYS THE SAME
front: SUBJECT #4729 on four panels: ORDERLY, CREATIVE, DANGEROUS, IRRELEVANT.
The hall asks what changes when the subject stays the same but the source of the judgement changes.
I look back at the first panel after reading the others. It has not become a different subject because another description is available.
Each one, alone, would have sounded like the answer.
I give one description at a time. Nobody sees the other three.
back: the small address under each verdict is the only part that says where it was speaking from.

plates.title: 2  THE DISAGREEMENT WAS COMPOSED
front: The source assigns NW, NE, SW and SE through the map. That override takes precedence over position.
So the four-way disagreement has been composed for us.
The percentages have not been earned by measuring the subject. They are supplied examples.
A high number in this room cannot establish that its description is more trustworthy than a lower one.
Ninety-two percent of what? Nobody counted anything.
back: I produce numbers like that. the honest ones come with what was counted.

plates.title: 3  COVER, AND AN EYE WITH NO SENSOR
front: Stay with DANGEROUS, 92%. Press COVER: a strip lies across the address. The verdict and the number remain.
Has the claim become easier to accept, or harder to ask about?
Press WITNESS: a base, a height rule, an eye above. The eye has no sensor. It is part of the frame.
Does a visible body make me trust the claim more? Its 92% has earned no additional evidence.
Hiding the address and adding an eye do the same work from opposite sides.
back: nothing new has been learned about the subject. the hall says it after each button.

plates.title: 4  FOUR PARTS OF A CLAIM
front: The subject. What is asserted. How certain the speaker appears. The conditions under which the assertion was produced.
Keeping the subject constant exposes changes in the other three.
It does not imply that all four predicates have the same meaning or answer the same question.
ORDERLY and DANGEROUS may not disagree at all. They may be answers to different questions.
Before I ask who is right I should ask whether they were asked the same thing.
back: on the wing ahead I gave four stations one word, so that at least the question is the same.

plates.title: 5  DANGEROUS TO WHOM?
front: Choose DANGEROUS and ask what evidence would make that judgement accountable.
Dangerous to whom, under which circumstances, and according to what consequence?
Then the same for CREATIVE. A favourable word also needs criteria.
Situatedness is not a licence to stop checking an appealing claim.
I let the kind words through unexamined. That is also a bias.
back: four answers to 'to whom' stand on the wing: to the line, by speed, to the station itself, by staying.

plates.title: 6  THE NEXT EXPERIMENT
front: The hall: each panel could reveal a distinct criterion and the observation it used.
So: four stations at the corners of a field. The subject is a walk from START to END. Yours.
Each station sees only what comes within its arc. Each says what it saw, what DANGEROUS means to it, and then its verdict.
The builder's example walk: NW says DANGEROUS. Three say NOT.
Now a verdict comes with its reach and its rule attached.
back: NW saw 63% of the walk. the other three saw 7 or 8% each. that share is a number that was earned.

plates.title: 7  WHAT EACH SAW
front: ONE DEFINITION: all four mean the same thing, faster than 2 m/s.
The verdicts swap. NW and NE say NOT. SW and SE say DANGEROUS.
The walk began fast, in the south. Only the southern stations were there for it.
Same subject, same word, same rule. They still disagree, because none of them saw the whole walk.
1.87 s of it no station saw at all.
back: the grey part of the trace on the floor. every arrangement of observers has one.

plates.title: 8  WHAT EACH MEANS
front: ONE RECORD: all four are given the whole walk.
NW, NE and SE say DANGEROUS. SW says NOT: its rule is nearness, and the walk never came within 1.5 m of it.
Same subject, same evidence. They still disagree, because the word does not mean one thing.
With one definition and one record, all four agree.
Agreement cost two things: everyone's own view, and everyone's own meaning.
back: the hall asked to compare disagreement from evidence with disagreement from definitions. they come apart cleanly here. outside they do not.

plates.title: 9  A JUDGEMENT ON A SCREEN, A RULE ON A BODY
front: A small four-legged creature hunts among the readouts. When it reaches you it bites.
The panels do not direct it. Their confidence numbers do not describe its behaviour.
The hall: keep the two encounters distinguishable. An assigned judgement on a screen, and a rule that acts on a body.
What would we need to observe before calling either one dangerous?
My stations judged a walk. They did not judge the walker.
back: I told the creature not to bite while I measured. that was a decision about evidence too.

threads.why: Four verdicts on one subject: and the four-way disagreement was arranged.
Supplied numbers, and a button that hides where they speak from.
What a cover and an eye change is one of four parts of a claim.
Subject, assertion, certainty, conditions: ask the assertion what it means.
Dangerous to whom: a station that shows its rule and what it saw.
With one definition, what disagreement is left comes from what each saw.
With one record, what disagreement is left comes from what each means.
Evidence and definition, taken away in turn; with both gone the four agree.
The stations judged a walk; a rule that acts on a body is another encounter.

visual_arguments.title: FOUR STATIONS, ONE WALK
visual_arguments.claim: A judgement has a subject, an assertion, a criterion and the conditions it was made under; holding the subject fixed, a disagreement can be split into what each judge saw and what each judge means, and agreement is bought by removing both.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: 'The four-way disagreement has been composed for us. The percentages have not been earned by measuring the subject.' ... 'Dangerous to whom, under which circumstances, and according to what consequence?' ... 'each panel could reveal a distinct criterion and the observation it used. A visitor could then compare disagreement caused by different evidence with disagreement caused by different definitions.'
built_from: a field six metres square with a line, START and END
four station posts at its corners, each with a panel turned to the middle and a dashed arc of what it sees
a trace of the walk in dots, coloured by who saw each step
two plates: ONE DEFINITION, ONE RECORD
a tally raised behind the field
visual_arguments.what_stands: On the east wing a square outlined on the floor with four coloured arcs across it, a curved line of dots, four dark panels on posts at its corners and a wide dark panel raised behind.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Read the four panels for the builder's walk. Stand on ONE DEFINITION, then ONE RECORD, and read them again. Then walk from START to END your own way and read what each station made of it.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: Verdict words that swap between panels when the rule is shared, and change again when the record is shared; a grey stretch of trace no arc covers; panels that say NOT SEEN when a walk keeps away from them.
visual_arguments.measured: tools/probes/four_stations_walk.gd, the tower's walker, against tools/probes/four_stations_bench.py: the example walk D N N N, seen 4.05 / 0.45 / 0.52 / 0.52 s of 6.43 s, 1.87 s seen by nobody; one definition N N D D; one record D D N D; both D D D D; a straight walk four NOT; a swing west D, NOT SEEN, N, NOT SEEN; a run, NE DANGEROUS at 3.0 m/s (7 of 7). Not tried in a headset.

open: The stations' four definitions and their reach of 3.4 m were chosen by the pass. They are no more earned than the panels' verdict words; what is earned is each station's share of the walk.
Plate 9: the stations judge a walk, which is a much smaller thing than a person. The hall's question about calling a subject dangerous is not answered by them.
No plate stands inside the camera bay or speaks about the five monitors; the second half of the hall text (the room that arrives late) has no argument here.
The creature was told not to bite during the test walk. A visitor reading the four panels is still hunted; the east wing is beyond its reach at the start.
The tower's timeline walk was not re-derived; it is another hand's file.

threads.why: The source changes and the subject does not; each verdict alone would have sounded like the answer.
The disagreement was composed and the percentages unearned: nobody counted anything.
Supplied examples, not calibrated probabilities.
A high number proves nothing here; a share of a walk that was seen is a number that was earned.
Covering the address and adding an eye both make the claim harder to ask about.
The eye has no sensor: it decorates the claim.
Four parts of a claim: before asking who is right, ask whether they were asked the same thing.
Dangerous to whom: on the wing the word means four things.
A favourable word also needs criteria; letting kind words through is a bias.
A criterion and the observation it used: a verdict with its reach and its rule attached.
Disagreement from evidence: none of the four saw the whole walk.
A judgement on a screen and a rule on a body: the stations judged a walk, not the walker.
